procedural_history.impugned_order: Validity of the Bombay Taluqdari Tenure Abolition Act, 1949
procedural_history.high_court_proceedings: Not explicitly mentioned, but implied that the challenge to the Act's validity was unsuccessful in a lower court, leading to the appeal.
procedural_history.supreme_court_posture: Appeals dismissed with costs, upholding the validity of the Bombay Taluqdari Tenure Abolition Act, 1949.

issue.issue_text: Whether the challenge to the validity of the Bombay Taluqdari Tenure Abolition Act, 1949, was maintainable.

facts: A challenge was brought against the validity of the Bombay Taluqdari Tenure Abolition Act, 1949.
law: The text references a legal provision which declares that certain "specified Acts" shall not be deemed void, or to have ever become void, on the ground that they violated certain rights.
This provision applies "notwithstanding any judgment, decree or order of any court or tribunal."
It further states that these specified Acts shall continue in force, subject to the power of a competent legislature to amend or repeal them.
application: The Supreme Court determined that the challenge to the validity of the Bombay Taluqdari Tenure Abolition Act, 1949, was not permissible or "not open."
This implies that the Act was one of the "specified Acts" protected by the overriding legal provision, which prevents courts from declaring it void on the grounds put forward by the challengers.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court held that the challenge to the validity of the Bombay Taluqdari Tenure Abolition Act, 1949, was not maintainable and, therefore, dismissed the appeals.

issue.issue_text: Whether an Indian court has jurisdiction under Section 188 of the Criminal Procedure Code to try a person for an offence committed in Pakistan, when at the time of the offence, the person had not yet migrated to or acquired the domicile of India.

facts: The accused, Ram Narain, was alleged to have committed an offense in Mailsi, a district that became part of Pakistan after the partition of India.
After the offense was committed, Ram Narain migrated from Pakistan to India, settled there, and acquired the status of an Indian citizen.
The East Punjab Government later sanctioned his prosecution in an Indian court for the offense committed in Pakistan.
law: The relevant laws are Section 4 of the Indian Penal Code (IPC) and Section 188 of the Criminal Procedure Code (CrPC).
These sections grant Indian courts jurisdiction over offenses committed by a 'citizen of India' even if the offense occurs outside India.

The court established the principle that acquiring citizenship or domicile in a country *after* committing an offense cannot retrospectively grant that country's courts jurisdiction to try the offense.
application: The Supreme Court determined that the critical factor for establishing jurisdiction under these laws is the status of the accused *at the time the offense was committed*.
The Attorney-General argued that because Ram Narain was an Indian citizen at the time of the prosecution, the court had jurisdiction. The Court rejected this argument.
The Court found that when the offense was committed in November 1947, Ram Narain was in Pakistan and had not yet migrated to or become a citizen of India.
Since he was not an Indian citizen at the time of the offense, the provisions of Section 4 IPC and Section 188 CrPC did not apply to him for an act committed outside India.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court concluded that an Indian court does not have jurisdiction to try a person for an offense committed in Pakistan if, at the time of the offense, that person was not a citizen of India. The subsequent migration to and acquisition of Indian citizenship by the accused does not retroactively grant jurisdiction to Indian courts.

issue.issue_text: Whether the Provincial Government had the power under Section 188 of the Criminal Procedure Code to sanction the prosecution of a person for an offence committed outside India at a time when that person was not domiciled in India.

facts: The accused, Ram Narain, was alleged to have committed an offence in November 1947 in a district that, after the partition of India, became part of Pakistan.
After committing the alleged offence, Ram Narain migrated to India and acquired Indian domicile and citizenship.
The East Punjab Government later sanctioned his prosecution in India for the offence committed in Pakistan.
law: The relevant laws are Section 4 of the Indian Penal Code and Section 188 of the Criminal Procedure Code.
These sections establish the principle that Indian courts have jurisdiction over offences committed by citizens of India, even if those offences occur outside of India.
application: The Court rejected the government's argument that jurisdiction could be based on the accused's citizenship at the time of the prosecution.
The Court held that the plain language of the sections requires the person to be a citizen of India *at the time the offence is committed*.
It reasoned that if the accused was not an Indian citizen or domiciled in India when the offence was committed, the provisions of these sections have no application.

The Court stated that acquiring Indian citizenship or domicile *after* the commission of the offence cannot retroactively grant jurisdiction to Indian courts for an act completed when the person was a foreigner.
At the time of the offence in November 1947, Ram Narain was in Pakistan and was not considered to be domiciled in India.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court concluded that the Provincial Government had no power under Section 188 of the Criminal Procedure Code to sanction the prosecution. This was because the jurisdiction of Indian courts depends on the accused's status at the time of the offence, and Ram Narain was not domiciled in India when the alleged crime was committed in Pakistan.

arguments.issue_text: Whether the challenge to the validity of the Bombay Taluqdari Tenure Abolition Act, 1949, was maintainable.
appellant_arguments: The Bombay Taluqdari Tenure Abolition Act, 1949, was invalid due to the violation of certain rights.
respondent_arguments: The challenge to the Act's validity was not maintainable because a subsequent provision declared that the Act shall not be deemed void, notwithstanding any court judgment, and shall continue in force.

arguments.issue_text: Whether an Indian court has jurisdiction under Section 188 of the Criminal Procedure Code to try a person for an offence committed in Pakistan, when at the time of the offence, the person had not yet migrated to or acquired the domicile of India.
appellant_arguments: The accused, Ram Narain, was a 'native Indian subject of Her Majesty' before August 15, 1947, and this status continued after that date, regardless of whether he was in India or Pakistan, making him subject to Indian jurisdiction.
The accused's intent to migrate to India was demonstrated by the fact that he had sent his family to India in October 1947, before the offence was committed.
respondent_arguments: An Indian court lacks jurisdiction because at the time of the offence, the accused had not yet landed on Indian soil, taken up permanent residence, or acquired the domicile of India.

arguments.issue_text: Whether the Provincial Government had the power under Section 188 of the Criminal Procedure Code to sanction the prosecution of a person for an offence committed outside India at a time when that person was not domiciled in India.
appellant_arguments: The government had the power to sanction the prosecution because the accused's status as a 'native Indian subject of Her Majesty' continued after partition, making him subject to Indian law for extraterritorial offences.
respondent_arguments: The government lacked the power to sanction the prosecution because Section 188 did not apply to the accused, as he was not domiciled in India when the offence was committed in Pakistan.

ratio_decidendi.ratio: A challenge to the validity of an Act is not permissible when a legislative provision declares that the specified Act shall not be deemed void, or to have ever become void, on particular grounds, notwithstanding any judgment, decree, or order of any court.
obiter: For the purpose of extra-territorial jurisdiction after August 15, 1947, the description 'Native subject of Her Majesty' became applicable only to residents of provinces within the boundaries of India.

judicial_reasoning.core_finding: For the purposes of extraterritorial criminal jurisdiction under Section 188 of the Criminal Procedure Code, a person's status is determined by their physical location and domicile at the time of the alleged offence. After the partition of India on August 15, 1947, the description 'Native subject of Her Majesty' became geographically specific, applying in India only to residents within its new boundaries. Consequently, an individual who was physically present in Pakistan and had not yet landed on Indian soil and taken up permanent residence there could not be considered domiciled in India, and thus could not be tried in an Indian court for an offence committed in Pakistan.
legal_tests_applied: The description 'Native subject of Her Majesty' after the 15th of August, 1947, became applicable in the territory now constituted India only to residents of provinces within the boundaries of India, and in Pakistan to residents of provinces within the boundaries of Pakistan.

Till the time that Ram Narain actually landed on the soil of India and took up permanent residence therein he cannot be described to be domiciled in India or even a Native Indian subject of His Majesty domiciled in India.
why_appellant_lost: The challenge to the validity of the Bombay Taluqdari Tenure Abolition Act, 1949, was not open because a subsequent provision declared that the Act shall not be deemed void 'notwithstanding any judgment, decree or order of any court or tribunal' and shall 'continue in force.'

The court rejected the argument that the status of 'native Indian subject of Her Majesty' continued to apply to the accused after partition regardless of his location, holding instead that this status became geographically specific to the new dominions of India and Pakistan.

The accused's intention to migrate to India, demonstrated by sending his family ahead, was insufficient to establish jurisdiction, as the determinative factor was his actual physical landing and establishment of permanent residence in India, which had not occurred at the time of the offence.
why_respondent_won: The court agreed that the challenge to the Bombay Taluqdari Tenure Abolition Act, 1949, was not maintainable due to a subsequent provision that retroactively validated the Act and declared it would continue in force.

The court accepted the respondent's argument that an Indian court lacked jurisdiction because at the time of the offence in Pakistan, the accused had not yet 'landed on the soil of India and took up permanent residence therein' and therefore could not be considered domiciled in India.

As the court found that the accused was not subject to its jurisdiction for an offence committed in Pakistan, it logically followed that the Provincial Government had no power under Section 188 of the Criminal Procedure Code to sanction his prosecution.
policy_considerations: The difficult circumstances of partition, such as the fact that Hindus and Sikhs were not safe in Pakistan and were under pressure to migrate, cannot be taken into consideration in determining the legal intention and domicile of a person for the purposes of establishing criminal jurisdiction.
